concepts.name: Definition and Classification of E-Waste under Indian Rules
key_dimensions: What qualifies as e-waste under E-Waste (Management) Rules 2016 vs 2022 amendment — inclusions and exclusions (e.g., lead-acid batteries excluded)
Difference between WEEE (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment) and e-waste in international vs Indian legal context
Categories of e-waste: Schedule I equipment list (ICT, consumer electricals, solar panels added in 2022)
UPSC trap: Solar PV panels were NOT covered in 2016 rules but were added later — a frequent factual question

concepts.name: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) Framework for E-Waste
key_dimensions: Core principle: polluter pays — producer is responsible for end-of-life collection and channelization
EPR obligations: targets, timelines, and the shift from weight-based to volume-based targets in 2022 rules
Role of Producer Responsibility Organizations (PROs) as intermediaries between producers and recyclers
UPSC trap: EPR under E-Waste Rules vs EPR under Plastic Waste Management Rules — overlapping but distinct frameworks with different nodal ministries and targets

concepts.name: E-Waste (Management) Rules 2016 vs 2022 Amendment: Key Changes
key_dimensions: Introduction of EPR certificate trading mechanism (market-based instrument) in 2022 — a first for e-waste
Inclusion of solar PV modules and their manufacturers under EPR obligations
Phased collection targets revised: 60% by 2023, 70% by 2024, 80% by 2025
UPSC trap: 2016 rules had deposit refund scheme provision which was dropped in 2022 — understanding what was retained vs removed

concepts.name: Roles and Responsibilities of Stakeholders under E-Waste Rules
key_dimensions: Producers vs Manufacturers vs Refurbishers vs Recyclers — legally distinct roles with different obligations
Bulk consumers (government, PSUs, hospitals) — mandatory channelization to authorized dismantlers/recyclers
Urban Local Bodies' role in collection infrastructure — often neglected angle
UPSC trap: Dealers and refurbishers have deposit collection duties but are NOT responsible for EPR targets — a common confusion point

concepts.name: Informal Sector in E-Waste Recycling: Scale, Hazards, and Integration
key_dimensions: India's informal sector handles ~90% of e-waste using primitive methods (acid baths, open burning) — health and environmental consequences
Geographical concentration: Moradabad, Mayapuri (Delhi), Dharavi (Mumbai), Shivakasi — prone to UPSC map-based questions
Why formal sector struggles to compete: cost disadvantage due to compliance costs vs informal zero-cost toxic processing
Policy challenge: integrating informal workers without displacement — just transition dimension, linkage to livelihoods and SDG 8

concepts.name: Hazardous Substances in E-Waste and Their Health/Environmental Impacts
key_dimensions: Key toxins: Lead (neurological damage), Mercury (Minamata disease link), Cadmium (renal toxicity), Hexavalent Chromium, PBDEs (endocrine disruptors)
Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS) compliance — Indian adaptation vs EU RoHS Directive
Soil and groundwater contamination pathways — leachate from landfills, acid drainage from informal recycling
UPSC trap: Distinguishing which substances are covered under E-Waste Rules' Schedule II (substances to be reduced) vs Hazardous Waste Management Rules

concepts.name: Urban Mining: Concept, Potential, and India's Critical Mineral Strategy
key_dimensions: Definition: recovering valuable metals (gold, silver, palladium, rare earth elements) from e-waste as a resource, not waste
India's e-waste contains more gold per tonne than primary gold ore — economic case for formal recycling
Linkage to Critical Mineral Mission 2023 — e-waste as domestic source for lithium, cobalt, nickel reducing import dependence
UPSC angle: Urban mining as circular economy strategy — connects to National Resource Efficiency Policy and SDG 12

concepts.name: Basel Convention and Its Relevance to E-Waste Trade
key_dimensions: Basel Convention 1989: controls transboundary movement of hazardous wastes — e-waste is a key category
Basel Ban Amendment (1995, entered into force 2019): prohibits export of hazardous waste from developed to developing countries
India's position: signatory to Basel but not the Ban Amendment — implications for e-waste import/export policy
UPSC trap: Distinction between Basel, Rotterdam (prior informed consent for chemicals), and Stockholm (POPs) Conventions — often tested together

concepts.name: EPR Certificate Trading Mechanism: Market-Based Instrument
key_dimensions: How it works: producers who exceed targets can sell surplus EPR certificates to those with deficits — creates a market for recycling
Administered through a centralized portal under MoEFCC — CPCB oversight
Analogy with Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) and Carbon Credits — UPSC loves cross-topic analogies
Limitation: risk of certificate fraud/greenwashing if physical recycling verification is weak — governance challenge

concepts.name: Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and State PCBs: Regulatory Roles in E-Waste
key_dimensions: CPCB: maintains national register of producers, authorizes PROs, monitors EPR compliance, publishes annual e-waste inventory
State PCBs: grant authorization to dismantlers and recyclers, conduct inspections, can suspend authorizations
UPSC trap: CPCB does NOT directly authorize recyclers — that is the role of State PCBs. A common confusion in MCQs
Conflict/overlap: When a producer operates nationally but recycler is state-level — jurisdictional complexity

concepts.name: India's E-Waste Generation: Statistics, Trends, and Global Context
key_dimensions: India is the 3rd largest e-waste generator globally (after China and USA) — ~3.2 million metric tonnes/year (Global E-waste Monitor 2024)
Only ~22% of global e-waste is formally recycled — India's formal recycling rate even lower (~5% estimated)
Fastest growing waste stream globally — driven by shorter product lifecycles and rising consumption
UPSC angle: India as both generator AND destination for illegal e-waste imports — dual vulnerability

concepts.name: Right to Repair Movement and Its Linkage to E-Waste Reduction
key_dimensions: Concept: consumers' right to repair products reduces premature disposal and e-waste generation — upstream prevention
India's Right to Repair Framework (2022) — Department of Consumer Affairs, covers electronics among other sectors
EU's Right to Repair Directive (2024) — comparison with India's approach, UPSC loves India vs global policy comparisons
UPSC trap: Right to Repair is under Consumer Affairs Ministry, NOT MoEFCC — interdepartmental jurisdiction angle

concepts.name: Circular Economy Principles Applied to E-Waste: Design for Environment
key_dimensions: Design for disassembly, modularity, and recyclability — reducing e-waste at source (upstream vs downstream approach)
India's National Resource Efficiency Policy (NREP) 2019 — resource efficiency targets and circular economy roadmap
Extended Product Lifecycle vs planned obsolescence — regulatory tension with industry practices
Linkage to SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption), SDG 9 (Industry Innovation), and SDG 13 (Climate — energy saved by recycling vs primary production)

concepts.name: E-Waste and Children's Health: Specific Vulnerabilities
key_dimensions: WHO reports on children working in informal e-waste recycling — exposure to neurotoxins during critical developmental stages
Child labour in e-waste dismantling — intersection with Child Labour (Prohibition) Act and e-waste regulations
Contamination of breast milk and placental transfer of e-waste toxins — intergenerational health equity issue
UPSC ethics/GS2 angle: State's obligation under CRC (Convention on Rights of the Child) to protect children from toxic occupations

concepts.name: E-Waste from Solar Panels: Emerging Challenge and Regulatory Gap
key_dimensions: India's solar capacity target (500 GW by 2030) will generate massive panel waste by 2035-2045 as panels reach end-of-life (25-year lifespan)
Solar panels added to E-Waste Rules 2022 — but recycling infrastructure for panels is nearly non-existent in India
Hazardous materials in panels: cadmium telluride (CdTe panels), lead solder, silicon dust
UPSC trap: Solar panel waste is now under E-Waste Rules, NOT under Solid Waste Management Rules — jurisdictional clarity question

concepts.name: E-Waste and Climate Change: Dual Relationship
key_dimensions: E-waste recycling saves energy vs virgin material extraction (recycling aluminium saves 95% energy) — mitigation co-benefit
Informal e-waste burning releases dioxins, furans, and black carbon — potent short-lived climate pollutants (SLCPs)
Recovery of refrigerants (HFCs) from discarded air conditioners/refrigerators — linkage to Kigali Amendment to Montreal Protocol
UPSC trap: HFC recovery from e-waste/old appliances falls under both E-Waste Rules AND Ozone Depleting Substances Rules — dual regulatory coverage

concepts.name: Digital Divide and E-Waste Justice: Equity Dimensions
key_dimensions: Developing nations receive disproportionate e-waste burden despite contributing least to digital consumption — environmental justice framing
Within India: e-waste recycling clusters in low-income urban areas (Dharavi, Seelampur) — NIMBY dynamics and environmental racism
Gender dimension: women and children disproportionately engaged in hazardous informal recycling tasks
UPSC GS2/Ethics angle: e-waste as a manifestation of structural inequality — connects to just transition and polluter-pays debates

concepts.name: Comparison of India's E-Waste Framework with EU's WEEE Directive
key_dimensions: EU WEEE Directive: mandatory take-back schemes, visible recycling fees on invoices, separate collection targets (65% of avg. equipment placed on market)
India's approach: EPR certificate trading (market mechanism) vs EU's more prescriptive deposit/take-back model
EU RoHS vs India's Schedule II of E-Waste Rules — similar substances restricted but India's enforcement is weaker
UPSC loves this comparison: India adopted EPR from EU model but chose market-based certificate trading over mandatory fee — policy choice implications

concepts.name: E-Waste Inventory and Data Governance Challenges in India
key_dimensions: CPCB publishes annual e-waste inventory — but actual generation estimates vary widely due to informal sector opacity
Lack of product registration data makes EPR target-setting unreliable — data deficit problem
Global E-Waste Monitor (UNU-ITU-ISWA) vs CPCB figures — discrepancies and their policy implications
UPSC trap: Who publishes the Global E-Waste Monitor? United Nations University (UNU) in partnership with ITU and ISWA — not UNEP, a common wrong answer

concepts.name: Scheduled Castes, Waste Pickers, and E-Waste: Social Dimensions of Waste Work
key_dimensions: Caste-based occupational segregation in waste work — Dalits overrepresented in hazardous e-waste dismantling
Kagad Kach Patra Kashtakari Panchayat (KKPKP) and similar waste picker organizations — advocacy for integration into formal EPR systems
National Policy on Solid Waste Management's acknowledgment of waste pickers vs E-Waste Rules' silence on their formal inclusion
UPSC GS2/Social Justice angle: whether EPR formalization excludes or empowers informal workers — policy design question with equity implications
